extraction.name: Vibravox
extraction.description: Vibravox is a GDPR-compliant dataset of French speech captured with body-conduction audio sensors, including two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone, plus an airborne microphone reference. It contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer, with annotations about recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions.
extraction.creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu (Laboratoire de Mécanique des Structures et des Systèmes Couplés, Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, HESAM Université; French-German Research Institute of Saint-Louis (ISL))
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected from 200 participants (188 retained after post-processing) who wore six audio sensors simultaneously while reading sentences from French Wikipedia and remaining silent under various acoustic conditions. Recordings were made in a 3D sound spatializer with a spherical array of 56 loudspeakers. The recording process consisted of four steps: speech-clean (15 minutes of sentence reading), speechless-noisy (2 minutes 24 seconds of silence in noisy environment), speechless-clean (54 seconds of silence), and speech-noisy (54 seconds of speech in noisy environment).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Some audio clips had shortcomings including mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from their initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, or instances where a microphone was inadvertently left unequipped. In some cases, such as when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, automatic filters were not triggered. Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained, with 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences excluded.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Audio recordings from six simultaneous sensors (headset microphone, forehead accelerometer, in-ear soft foam microphone, in-ear rigid earpiece microphone, throat microphone, temple vibration pickup) recorded at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution using a Zoom F8n field recorder. Text stimuli sourced from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: VAD timestamps generated by Voice Activity Detection (VAD) are extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides. In rare cases where the adjusted start or end timestamps exceed the original audio boundaries, the audio is trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side. The dataset is split by speaker, with 80% of male and female speakers in the training set, 10% in the development/validation set, and 10% in the test set.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter is uniformly applied to each acquisition channel. Three automatic filters were applied to remove utterances with obvious deficiencies: (1) PER > 10% filter using Levenshtein distance between labeled and Whisper-derived phonetic transcriptions; (2) SNR filter requiring Lspeech_50 - Lsilence_50 > 1.5 dB; (3) sensitivity drift filter checking Lspeech_50 > Lsilence_50. Text was filtered to exclude proper names (except common first names, French town/region/country names), numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, and syntactic errors, followed by lowercasing and punctuation removal.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Phonetic transcriptions were generated using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) with the text phonemizer of the CoML lab. For words where the phonemizer produced language switches, manual phonetic transcription was performed. Recording condition annotations were also included.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Phoneme Error Rate (PER) was computed using the Levenshtein distance between the labeled phonetic transcription and the phonetic transcription derived from Whisper's output to verify annotation quality. Samples with PER > 10% were discarded.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: whisper-timestamped (speech-to-text engine based on Whisper with dynamic time warping for word timestamps); text phonemizer of the CoML lab (for IPA phonetic transcription)
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender information is collected; participants are categorized as female or male. Voice biometric data is collected.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset enables research in robust communication systems for noisy environments including military and industrial applications. It also raises considerations about biometric data use for access control and intelligence gathering.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is limited to French language. A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants to increase representativeness and inclusivity.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes as it lacks a clean reference under noisy conditions. Some participants' ear canals were too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing. The Lombard effect causes speakers to increase vocal effort in noisy conditions, meaning reported signal-to-external-noise ratios represent a lower bound. The dataset is only in French.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing for speech enhancement (bandwidth extension), automatic speech recognition (speech-to-phonemes), and speaker verification tasks. The speechless-clean subset can be used for heart rate tracking or analyzing noise properties of sensors. The dataset can also be used to generate synthetic datasets with realistic physiological noise.

name.evidence: Vibravox is a dataset compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) containing audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors

description.evidence: Vibravox is a dataset compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) containing audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors: two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone. The dataset also includes audio data from an airborne microphone used as a reference. The Vibravox corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer.

inLanguage.evidence: The absence of publicly available BCM datasets in French, restricting research primarily to the languages covered by existing resources.

isLiveDataset.evidence: This highly curated dataset, comprising four subsets — speech-clean, speech-noisy, speechless-clean, and speechless-noisy — is now publicly available.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: The recording process consists of four steps that are performed consecutively for each participant in the order listed below. Each of these steps corresponds to a subset of the Vibravox dataset.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: Creating the Vibravox BCM dataset involved a number of different tasks. These included designing pre-amplification and conditioning circuits for each transducer, coding the frontend and back-end software for the recording user interface, adapting the housings and fixings for some audio sensors to the human body through 3D modeling and printing, and selecting transducer technologies and recording parameters.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: a small number of audio clips had various shortcomings: although we carefully monitored and validated each recording during the experimental process, the workflow was not entirely foolproof. Mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from their initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, or instances where a microphone was inadvertently left unequipped led to some data inconsistencies.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: The Zoom F8n records all six sensor signals simultaneously, operates at a sampling rate of 48 kHz and a resolution of 32 bits, thereby guaranteeing precise signal capture with high fidelity. The text utilized for participant readings originates from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: the timestamps generated by Voice Activity Detection (VAD) are extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides. In rare cases where the adjusted start or end timestamps exceed the original audio boundaries, the audio is trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side. The dataset is then split by speaker, with 80% of male and female speakers in the training set, 10% in the development/validation set, and 10% in the test set.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: we applied a series of three automatic filters to remove utterances with obvious deficiencies. We retained only sentences with correct pronunciation and a sufficiently high SNR, based on predefined criteria outlined in Figure 2. To enhance audio data quality, a 20 Hz high-pass filter is uniformly applied to each acquisition channel, effectively attenuating low-frequency noise and artifacts.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: From this normalized text, we also generated the corresponding phonetic transcription using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), which contains 33 phonemes in French. This operation was done with the text phonemizer of the CoML lab. A phase of manual phonetic transcription was then necessary for these unrecognized words, such as 'algorithme'.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: PER[j]: Phoneme Error Rate is computed for each sample j using the Levenshtein distance between the phonetic labeled transcription and the phonetic transcription derived from Whisper's output. The first filter discards any audio samples where PER[j] > 10%.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: The whisper-timestamped model constitutes a key component of our indicator extraction process. This model is a speech-to-text engine based on Whisper that applies dynamic time warping to cross-attention weights. This operation was done with the text phonemizer of the CoML lab.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: The dataset is then split by speaker, with 80% of male and female speakers in the training set, 10% in the development/validation set, and 10% in the test set. Total: 97F/91M

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: One such application is access control, where it can strengthen security by adding an extra layer compared to conventional methods like keycards or codes. Another compelling application lies in intelligence gathering. By pinpointing known voices in intercepted transmissions, speaker identification can reveal the involvement of high-value targets.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: to increase the representativeness and inclusivity of the dataset, a deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: the speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes, as it lacks a clean reference under such conditions. However, in some cases, such as when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, these filters were not triggered. the Lombard effect causes speakers to increase their vocal effort in noisy conditions, meaning the reported signal-to-external-noise ratios represent a lower bound on the actual values.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We conducted a series of experiments on various speech-related tasks, including speech recognition, speech enhancement, and speaker verification. These samples can be valuable for tasks such as heart rate tracking or simply analyzing the noise properties of the various sensors. It could also be conveniently used to generate synthetic datasets with realistic physiological (and sensor-inherent) noise captured by body-conduction audio sensors.
